standard.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
standard.description: investigate Newton's laws of motion and quantitatively analyse the relationship between force, mass and acceleration of objects
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can represent and explain how balanced and unbalanced forces, including gravity, relate to changes in an object's motion in terms of mass, magnitude and direction (AC9S7U04). There is a two-year gap in the physical sciences strand (Years 8–9 address energy, not force/motion), so force and motion knowledge has had no curriculum reinforcement for three years. Students carry the Aristotelian misconception that moving objects require a continuous applied force to maintain motion. They have no prior exposure to Newton's named laws, acceleration as a defined quantity, F=ma as a quantitative relationship, or action-reaction pairs.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students apply Newton's three laws of motion to analyse object behaviour and quantitatively solve problems using F=ma, including multi-force scenarios, free body diagrams, and real-world applications such as vehicle safety features and sport.

nodes.label: Force as a vector quantity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can represent forces as vectors with both magnitude and direction, and add or subtract forces acting along a single axis to find net force.
nodes.minimum_width: Students represent a named force as an arrow showing magnitude and direction, and calculate net force for two forces acting along the same line.
nodes.typical_width: Students represent multiple forces on a single object; calculate net force for forces in the same and opposite directions; distinguish between contact and non-contact forces; use consistent sign conventions for direction.
wider: Represent forces on objects in two dimensions and estimate resultant direction — what happens when forces are not perfectly aligned?
Investigate how First Nations Australians' use of spearthrowers applies directional force principles to achieve greater projectile speed and impact

response_modes.reason: Students covered force magnitude and direction at Year 7, but three years without reinforcement means vector representation and sign conventions are likely degraded. This node re-establishes the representational tools that all quantitative work in N4 and N6 depends on — precision here prevents systematic sign errors throughout.

success_criteria: Represents a named force as a vector with a labelled magnitude and direction
Calculates net force for two forces acting along the same axis using a consistent sign convention
Distinguishes between contact forces (friction, normal) and non-contact forces (gravity)

nodes.label: Newton's First Law — inertia and the Aristotelian misconception
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can state Newton's First Law and explain why a moving object with no net force continues at constant velocity, identifying and correcting the misconception that motion requires a continuous force.
nodes.minimum_width: Students state that an object continues at constant velocity (or remains at rest) when the net force is zero, and explain one everyday scenario where this is counterintuitive (e.g. a sliding hockey puck).
nodes.typical_width: Students apply Newton's First Law to multiple scenarios including objects at rest and in constant motion; explain inertia as resistance to change in motion; describe how friction explains why objects appear to slow down without a visible opposing force; connect to balanced force concept from Year 7.
wider: Analyse why inertia makes seatbelts necessary — trace what happens to an unrestrained passenger when a car stops suddenly
Investigate historical resistance to Galileo's and Newton's ideas — why was the Aristotelian view so persistent, and what evidence overturned it?
nodes.hinge_reason: The Aristotelian misconception — that motion requires a continuous force — directly undermines Newton's Second and Third Laws if unresolved. Students who hold this view interpret F=ma as 'force produces motion' rather than 'net force produces change in motion', causing systematic errors in N4 and N6. Students who cannot separate constant velocity from acceleration also cannot correctly define acceleration in N3.

response_modes.reason: The Aristotelian misconception is well-documented and persistent — it survives exposure to the correct definition without explicit confrontation. Students need scenarios where the intuitive 'force causes motion' framing produces a wrong prediction, followed by correction using Newton's First Law. Friction as the hidden force explains almost every everyday 'counterexample' students produce.

success_criteria: States Newton's First Law correctly
Explains why a moving object without net force continues at constant velocity (does not slow down)
Identifies friction as the hidden force responsible for observed deceleration in everyday scenarios
Corrects the claim that 'a moving object needs a force to keep moving'

nodes.label: Acceleration as a defined vector quantity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity, calculate acceleration from velocity and time data, and represent acceleration as a vector with direction.
nodes.minimum_width: Students calculate acceleration using a = Δv/t for a single scenario and state the direction of acceleration relative to net force.
nodes.typical_width: Students calculate acceleration from distance-time and velocity-time graphs; distinguish between speeding up, slowing down and changing direction as forms of acceleration; explain deceleration as acceleration in the direction opposite to motion; apply correct units.
wider: Construct and interpret velocity-time graphs from motion sensor data, reading acceleration from the gradient
Explain why a car travelling at constant speed around a curve is still accelerating — and predict the direction of the net force required
nodes.hinge_reason: Acceleration is used in every subsequent quantitative context. Students who conflate acceleration with speed, or who cannot assign direction to acceleration, produce systematic errors in F=ma calculations (N4), multi-force problems (N6), and all real-world applications (N7). The shift from everyday language ('speeding up') to a defined vector quantity is a representation change that does not happen incidentally.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Graphical interpretation of motion (velocity-time graphs, distance-time graphs) is genuinely rich and directly supported by the elaborations. Investment here — reading acceleration from gradient, building graphs from data — eliminates systematic errors in all downstream quantitative work and develops the mathematical representation skills the descriptor explicitly demands.

response_modes.reason: Acceleration must shift from an everyday colloquial term to a defined vector quantity with units. Students who passed Year 7 with a qualitative understanding ('unbalanced forces change motion') need this redefinition made explicit before F=ma is introduced — otherwise they substitute intuitive acceleration for the defined quantity in calculations.

Multiple representational contexts — data tables, velocity-time graphs, motion sensor outputs — build the mathematical literacy the descriptor's 'quantitatively analyse' demand requires. Each context exercises the same defined quantity from a different angle.

success_criteria: Defines acceleration as the rate of change of velocity with correct units (m/s²)
Calculates acceleration from velocity and time data
States the direction of acceleration and identifies it as the same direction as net force
Distinguishes acceleration from speed — identifies deceleration and direction change as forms of acceleration

nodes.label: Newton's Second Law — F = ma
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply F = ma to calculate force, mass or acceleration in single-force scenarios and explain qualitatively how changing mass or force affects acceleration.
nodes.minimum_width: Students correctly apply F = ma to solve for one unknown (F, m, or a) in a single-force scenario with correct units.
nodes.typical_width: Students solve F = ma for all three variables across multiple contexts; explain proportional relationships (double the force → double the acceleration; double the mass → halve the acceleration); use graphs to represent F–a relationships at constant mass; apply correct units throughout.
wider: Investigate the F–a relationship experimentally using trolleys and hanging masses; plot results and assess linearity
Analyse the force required to bring a vehicle to a stop within a given distance — connect to the elaboration on speed limits near schools
nodes.hinge_reason: F = ma is the quantitative engine of all subsequent nodes. Students who cannot reliably apply the relationship — particularly students who confuse net force with applied force, or who drop direction — cannot solve multi-force problems (N6) or analyse real-world applications (N7). Errors introduced here propagate into every calculation context.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: F = ma is the most elaboration-rich node in this standard. Experimental investigation, graphical analysis, vehicle safety calculations, and athletic performance analysis are all genuine width contexts that the elaborations explicitly name. Investment here is high-leverage for the quantitative demand of the descriptor.

response_modes.reason: Procedural fluency with F = ma — correct formula rearrangement, unit tracking, direction assignment — is a prerequisite for multi-force work. Students need practice and self-correction at the single-force level before net force scenarios are introduced.

The elaborations name multiple distinct application contexts: vehicle stopping distances, athlete performance, driverless vehicle braking. Each applies F = ma to a different object with different known and unknown quantities — genuine width rather than repeated practice.

success_criteria: Correctly applies F = ma to solve for force, mass or acceleration in a single-force scenario
Uses correct units (N, kg, m/s²) and maintains direction consistency
Explains qualitatively how doubling force or mass affects acceleration

nodes.label: Newton's Third Law — action-reaction pairs
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify action-reaction force pairs in a scenario and explain why they do not cancel, despite being equal and opposite.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify the action and reaction forces in one scenario (e.g. foot pushing on ground, ground pushing back on foot) and explain that they act on different objects.
nodes.typical_width: Students identify action-reaction pairs across multiple scenarios (rocket thrust, swimming, jumping); explain why the pairs do not cancel using the 'different objects' principle; distinguish Third Law pairs from balanced forces acting on the same object.
wider: Analyse propulsion in a rocket, jet engine or swimmer using Newton's Third Law — predict direction and relative magnitude of each force pair
Investigate a common Third Law misconception: 'the heavier object exerts more force' — design a demonstration that tests this prediction

response_modes.reason: The persistent Third Law misconception — that equal and opposite forces cancel and therefore nothing should move — must be addressed by explicitly establishing that action-reaction pairs act on different objects. Scenarios where only one object is being analysed (e.g. a person jumping) help isolate the relevant force before students encounter multi-body analysis.

success_criteria: Identifies the action and reaction forces in a named scenario and states which object each acts on
Explains why action-reaction pairs do not cancel (they act on different objects)
Distinguishes Third Law pairs from balanced forces acting on the same object

nodes.label: Multi-force analysis and free body diagrams
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can draw a free body diagram for an object with multiple forces and calculate net force, then apply F = ma to determine acceleration.
nodes.minimum_width: Students draw a free body diagram for a scenario with two or three forces and calculate net force and resulting acceleration.
nodes.typical_width: Students apply free body diagrams to objects at rest, constant velocity, and accelerating; include normal force, friction, gravity, and applied force; calculate net force and acceleration for multi-step scenarios; explain how airbags, seatbelts and crumple zones extend stopping time to reduce force.
wider: Analyse a vehicle collision scenario: given stopping distance and mass, calculate impact force with and without crumple zone — evaluate the safety benefit quantitatively
Design a free body diagram for a multi-phase motion (e.g. a rocket launching then coasting) — identify when each law applies and when net force changes
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Free body diagrams connect all three laws in a single representational tool and the vehicle safety elaboration is a rich, socially relevant application context. The quantitative safety analysis (crumple zones, airbags) is a genuine extension that does not accelerate content.

response_modes.reason: Free body diagrams become meaningful across varied force configurations — not just 'a box on a table' but objects on inclines, in vehicles, in sport contexts. Width here builds the representational flexibility students need for unseen problems.

success_criteria: Draws a correctly labelled free body diagram for an object with at least three forces
Calculates net force and resulting acceleration from a free body diagram
Applies the result to explain a real-world scenario (e.g. vehicle safety, sport)

nodes.label: Quantitative problem solving — integrating all three laws
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can solve multi-step force and motion problems that require selecting and applying Newton's laws, using mathematical representations including graphs and algebraic formulas.
nodes.minimum_width: Students solve a two-step problem that requires applying at least two of Newton's laws and uses both F = ma and a kinematic relationship (e.g. a = Δv/t).
nodes.typical_width: Students solve multi-step problems across contexts: vehicles, athletes, objects under gravity; select appropriate laws and formulas; represent solutions graphically; construct arguments supported by quantitative data (e.g. speed limit near schools); check reasonableness of answers.
wider: Construct a data-supported argument for a lower speed limit in a school zone — include stopping distance calculations and force analysis at different speeds
Investigate how driverless vehicle braking systems apply Newton's laws — what sensor data and calculations does the system need to brake in time?

response_modes.reason: Multi-step problem solving requires procedural fluency across several interconnected relationships. Students need structured practice selecting the right law for each step, tracking units across calculations, and checking answers for physical reasonableness before assessment-level problems.

success_criteria: Solves a multi-step problem applying at least two of Newton's laws with correct units throughout
Uses mathematical representations (graphs or algebraic formulas) to support a quantitative argument
Checks the reasonableness of a calculated answer in physical terms

nodes.label: Real-world applications — Newton's laws in context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply Newton's laws to analyse motion in real-world contexts including vehicle safety, sport, and First Nations technologies, and explain design decisions in terms of force, mass and acceleration.
nodes.minimum_width: Students apply at least one of Newton's laws to explain a design feature or technique in a real-world context (e.g. why airbags reduce injury, why a longer spearthrower increases projectile speed).
nodes.typical_width: Students analyse multiple application contexts connecting Newton's laws to design intent; explain how spearthrowers extend force application time and distance to achieve greater acceleration; evaluate safety features quantitatively; compare athletic techniques in terms of force, mass and acceleration; connect to elaboration contexts (sport, driverless vehicles, First Nations technologies).
wider: Investigate a specific First Nations throwing technology (spearthrower or bow) and analyse the force-extension mechanism using Newton's Second and Third Laws
Propose and justify a design modification to a vehicle safety feature using Newton's laws — what change would improve occupant protection, and why?
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The elaborations explicitly name a wide range of authentic contexts — First Nations technologies, sport, vehicle safety, driverless vehicles — that are all genuine width rather than repetition. Students applying Newton's laws across culturally and technologically varied contexts develop the flexible application the descriptor's 'investigate' and 'analyse' demands require.

response_modes.reason: This node is the full descriptor demand: students bringing all three laws together to investigate and explain motion in contexts not previously analysed. The integration is across laws (selecting the right one), representations (quantitative, diagrammatic, verbal), and contexts (cultural, technological, sporting).

The elaborations name contexts that are genuinely distinct — First Nations spearthrowers, airbags, driverless braking, sport. Each offers a different force configuration and a different design question. This is width, not depth — students are applying the same laws to new situations, not learning new physics.

success_criteria: Applies at least two of Newton's laws to explain a design feature or technique in a real-world context
Explains a First Nations throwing technology in terms of force, time of application and resulting acceleration
Evaluates a vehicle safety feature quantitatively using Newton's Second Law
